summary: Solid, family-friendly core found across many sources. Hanal Pixán ('food of the souls') is the Yucatec Maya Day of the Dead of the Yucatán Peninsula. It runs over three days: 31 October for the souls of children, 1 November for the souls of adults, 2 November a mass for all souls at the cemetery. Families clean the house, set a table altar with photos, candles, flowers, water and the favorite foods of their loved ones, and cook mucbipollo (pib), a big tamal baked in an underground oven (píib). Families believe the souls come to visit and 'eat' the food; afterwards the living share it. The tone is remembrance and love, not fear. Sourcing is tourism-board, news, cultural-blog and encyclopedic (no peer-reviewed paper found), but the core is consistent across sources.
facts: Hanal Pixán means 'food of the souls': hanal = food/meal, pixán = soul/spirit. It is the Maya name for the Day of the Dead in the Yucatán Peninsula. [yucatan.travel; naatikmexico; aldeacoba; yucatantoday; Mexico News Daily 253467]

Main window is 31 October to 2 November, three consecutive days. Day 1 (31 Oct): children who died. Day 2 (1 Nov): adults who died. Day 3 (2 Nov): all souls, with a mass (misa pixán), usually at the local cemetery. [yucatan.travel; aldeacoba; MND 253467; mexicodesconocido; yucatanliving; Por Esto]

Maya names of the days: u hanal palal (children's food, 31 Oct), u hanal nucuch uinicoob (adults' food, 1 Nov), u hanal pixanoob or misa pixán (all souls, 2 Nov). [aldeacoba; Por Esto/posta/magicaltowns snippets]

Families believe the dead are allowed to visit the living in these days and come back to their old homes and families; altars and food welcome them. [yucatan.travel; aldeacoba; mexicodesconocido; yucatanliving]

The celebration is about remembering and honoring loved ones, not sadness or fear. It is described as different from Halloween, and in Yucatán the dead do not 'dance in the streets' as in some other parts of Mexico. [naatikmexico; mexicodesconocido; yucatantoday]

Families get ready for days, some from the start of October: they cook, build the altar and clean the house and yard (some say so the souls do not need to tidy up). Graves are cleaned, weeds removed, tombs painted. [yucatantoday; MND 127110; yucatanliving]

The altar is a table, often with a white or embroidered tablecloth (white for adults, colorful for children). Items: photos of the departed, candles, flowers, incense (copal), food and drink, a green wooden cross, and water and salt. [yucatan.travel; yucatantoday; Por Esto; MND 127110]
The green cross on the altar represents the ceiba, the sacred tree of life (yaxché in Maya). [yucatan.travel; Por Esto; MND 127110]

Candles light the way for the souls to come to the altar and to find the way home; candles are also lined along paths and at doors. White candles for adults, colored candles for children. [MND 127110; mexicodesconocido; Por Esto; yucatantoday]

Flowers: the yellow-orange marigold, called xpujuc in Maya (Spanish cempasúchil, from Nahuatl 'twenty flowers'), is used on altars to guide the souls. Other flowers named: xté (red), virginias, wildflowers. [mexicodesconocido; Por Esto; naatikmexico; Wikipedia Day of the Dead; yucatantoday]
Children's altars: bright colors, colored candles, toys, sweets, chocolate, bread, mazapán, fruit. [yucatan.travel; mexicodesconocido; yucatanliving]

Adults' altars: white candles, the person's favorite foods and drinks (some sources add tobacco, mezcal or balché); personal items such as work tools. [mexicodesconocido; yucatanliving; posta snippet]

Mucbipollo (also mukbil pollo, pib) is the star dish: a large tamal of corn dough (masa) filled with chicken and/or pork in a sauce (k'óol) made from broth, achiote and masa, wrapped in banana leaves. [yucatan.travel; yucatantoday; yucatan.com.mx; Wikipedia Day of the Dead; Wikipedia Píib]

It is cooked underground: a hole is dug, stones and wood are heated with fire, the wrapped tamales go in, are covered with leaves and earth, and cook about 1.5 to 2 hours. The oven is called píib (pib). Today many families use a home oven or a bakery. [yucatan.com.mx; Wikipedia Píib; MND 127110; yucatantoday; mexicodesconocido]
mukbil means 'buried'; the dish name mixes Maya (mukbil) and Spanish (pollo, chicken). [yucatan.travel; Wikipedia Píib; yucatan.com.mx]
Families cook together and each person has a role; each family has its own recipe. In remote villages people move stones and dig the hole for the pib. [mexicodesconocido; yucatantoday]
After the souls have 'eaten' the essence of the food, the living family eats it and shares it with relatives and friends. [yucatantoday; MND 253467; Wikipedia Day of the Dead (general belief)]

Other typical foods: xec (fruit salad of jícama, orange, mandarin, grapefruit, with chili or lime), atole (sweet corn drink), hot chocolate, tamales, candied pumpkin, fruit, sweets, bread for children, pibinal (corn cooked in the píib). [yucatanliving; yucatantoday; mexicodesconocido; yucatan.com.mx; Por Esto]
Yucatán altars usually do not include pan de muerto, unlike central Mexico. [Por Esto differences; Por Esto ofrenda maya]
Chachac waj (red tamal made with achiote, also cooked in the píib) is another special dish of these days. [MND 127110; Wikipedia Píib; yucatanliving]

Some days later (about a week, or the last day of the month, depending on village) comes the closing gathering called bix / mes biix / ochavario: prayers, a special meal, and candles or a line of light at the doors to guide the souls back. [yucatanliving; MND 253467; yucatantoday; Por Esto ofrenda maya]

The tradition blends Maya beliefs about death as part of a cycle with Spanish Catholic customs (fixed dates, mass, cross, altars). Souls were seen as immortal. [yucatan.travel; aldeacoba; mexicodesconocido]

State and city governments promote it with altar exhibitions and the Festival de las Ánimas / Paseo de las Ánimas in Mérida (Paseo begun 2008 per Yucatan Living and México Desconocido). [yucatanliving; mexicodesconocido; MND 253467; Por Esto]
variants: Spelling of the name: Hanal Pixán (common, Spanish-style) vs Janal Pixán / Janal Pixáan (INALI standard orthography since 2014, per Yucatán Today). Use Hanal Pixán in the story with a one-time note that Janal is the newer Maya spelling.

Dates of children vs adults: majority say 31 Oct = children, 1 Nov = adults, 2 Nov = all souls. A LAPL page swaps them (1 Nov children, 2 Nov adults) and is likely an error. Naatik says children are welcomed on the night of 31 Oct into 1 Nov and adults the night of 1 Nov into 2 Nov. Yucatán Today says the souls stay among the living throughout November. Wikipedia says some places also mark 6 November.

Maya day names are assigned differently: México Desconocido uses Chichán Pixán (small soul) for children and Nohoch Pixán (big soul) for adults; Yucatan Living uses Mehen/Chichán Pixán and Nohoch Pixán; Aldea Cobá and others use u hanal palal and u hanal nucuch uinicoob. Prefer u hanal palal / u hanal nucuch uinicoob.
Content of 2 Nov: most say mass for all souls; México Desconocido says special prayers and a small separate altar for 'ánimas solas' (souls with no family).

Altar structure: some say a simple table; Por Esto and Yucatán Today say three levels for modern altars; México Desconocido lists seven jícaras; one blog says three altars (children, adults, all souls). Core is the same: table, photos, candles, flowers, food, cross.

Flower: México Desconocido and Por Esto equate xpujuc with cempasúchil; Yucatán Today lists xté, xpujuk, jmul and wildflowers; Por Esto's 'differences' article lists cempasúchil only for central Mexico. Safe wording: 'yellow and orange flowers called xpujuc (marigold)'.
Bix timing: about 8 days later / 8 or 9 November (Yucatan Living, Por Esto) vs 'one week after' (MND) vs last day of November (Yucatán Today). Say 'a few days to a week later in many villages'.

Pib vs mucbipollo: used interchangeably in most sources. Strictly, píib is the underground oven and the Maya word also used for the dish; Wikipedia notes many Mexicans call the tamales cooked in it 'pib' while the tamal is chachak waaj. A priest quoted by yucatan.com.mx says the original name is 'pib xcaac' (hen cooked in an oven).
Cooking time: about 1 hour (MND 127110), about 1.5 hours for chicken (Wikipedia Píib), about 2 hours (yucatan.com.mx).
Where altars sit: at home (most), under trees at graves (MND 253467), in the cemetery on 2 Nov.

cautions: Religion and death: keep the tone gentle. Say 'families believe' or 'the Maya believe' rather than stating that souls literally return. Do not describe how anyone died. For the children's day, speak softly (little ones who are no longer here) and avoid scary images; no skulls, skeletons or ghosts (not typical of Yucatán Hanal Pixán per sources).

Do not present it as purely pre-Hispanic. Sources describe a blend of Maya beliefs and Spanish Catholic customs (mass, cross, fixed dates). The origins of Day of the Dead in general are debated by scholars (Wikipedia). Hedge any 'ancient' claim.

Do not equate it with central-Mexico Día de Muertos: Yucatán altars have no pan de muerto and no dancing skeletons; Catrinas and sugar skulls are modern and not traditionally Maya (Mis in MND 127110; México Desconocido). Do not use 'Mictlán' for the Maya underworld (Por Esto does, but Mictlán is Nahua; the Maya underworld is Xibalbá per Aldea Cobá). Safest: avoid naming an underworld.
Alcohol and tobacco on adult altars (balché, mezcal, cigarettes) are reported; omit them or keep to 'favorite food and drink' in a beginner family story.

Single-source or interpretive claims to avoid as fact: 'the four legs of the altar are four gods' (MND 127110), 'seven jícaras = men in the milpa and girls at the comal' (México Desconocido), 'jícaras = nine gods of the underworld' (Por Esto), 'serpent-shaped paths' and 'pib is the only dish the dead can take back' (Yucatán Today), 'pib exists only on the peninsula' (tourism claim), 'digging the hole = burial, taking food out = souls' return' (MND 127110 interpretation).

Folk taboos (mirrors removed, animals tied up, no sewing or hunting, children's red or black wrist ribbon) appear in only one or two sources (MND 127110, Yucatan Living) and vary by village. Use at most one, hedged: 'in some villages'.
Exact dates vary by village and source: say 'from 31 October to 2 November' and 'in some places the days continue through November'. Bix timing varies (about a week later vs end of November).

Spelling is contested: Hanal vs Janal; píib/pib/pibil; chachac waj / chachak waaj; k'óol / kol; xpujuc / x'pujuc / xpujuk. Pick one set and keep it consistent; mention once that the newer Maya spelling uses J.
Pomuch bone-cleaning (Campeche) appears in one source (MND 253467); it is a local custom and sensitive; do not include it in a beginner story.

Sources are tourism boards, news, cultural blogs and encyclopedic pages. The National Museum of Mexican Art page is only a packet blurb; no peer-reviewed article or government heritage record was found. Magical Towns (magicaltowns.mx), Posta and LAPL were seen only as search-engine snippets (fetch failed or not attempted); their details are used only where fetched sources agree.
Wikipedia has no dedicated Hanal Pixán page (the URL redirects to Day of the Dead); it only mentions Hanal Pixan briefly (Belize note) and in the Píib article.
